title: Life Under the Parental Eye of Sauron
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Katherine Martinko draws on her teenage experience living under a hyper-surveillant guardian to make a case against parental location-tracking of children and teens. She argues that constant monitoring — enabled by smartphone apps — conveys a message of distrust that backfires in measurable ways: research shows tracked teens make worse personal-safety decisions (outsourcing responsibility to parents), are more secretive, and are pushed toward unsupervised online spaces that carry far greater risks than the physical world. Martinko also flags a troubling cultural precedent: by teaching children that love and surveillance go together, parents are normalising what in other relationships would be recognised as controlling behaviour. She calls on parents to wean themselves off tracking apps, defend children's right to privacy, and trust children with increasing autonomy proportional to their demonstrated trustworthiness.
points: Research shows that teens who know they are being tracked by parents tend to make poorer personal-safety decisions — they appear to abdicate responsibility, assuming their parents can always locate and rescue them.

A Dutch survey found tracked teens were more likely to engage in secretive behaviour and share less information with parents about friends and activities — the surveillance backfires by encouraging exactly the opacity parents are trying to prevent.

By normalising location-sharing between parents and children, parents are modelling to their kids that surrendering privacy to anyone who claims to love them is acceptable — a behavioural norm that maps dangerously onto future intimate relationships.

Pew Research (2024) found 42% of parents track adult children aged 18-24 — an astonishing figure that illustrates how tracking that begins innocuously in childhood fails to terminate when children become capable adults.

Recess from surveillance is an equity issue: children in safer, resource-rich families can recover lost autonomy elsewhere, but for many children school is the only reliable context for supervised-but-free play, making tracking especially harmful for those most dependent on structured freedom.
quotes: There is alarming research that shows that teens who know their parents are tracking them tend to make poorer decisions when it comes to personal safety. It's as if they abdicate responsibility for themselves, assuming that their parent can always find them and get them out of any sticky situation.

A survey in the Netherlands found that teens whose parents tracked them were more likely to engage in secretive behaviours and provide fewer details about their friends, activities, and social lives than teens whose parents did not track them. It suggests that the more a teen feels their privacy is being invaded, the more they want to hide information, which ultimately backfires on the parent.

By tracking our kids, we're essentially telling them that it is acceptable to surrender their privacy to anyone who claims to love them, whether it's ourselves or their friends or future lovers. And that's not OK!

Now controlling behavior among intimate partners resembles nothing so much as just another day with a helicopter parent, with an expectation that location sharing and read receipts are turned on. Surveillance keeps us all safe, after all. 'It's for your own good!' It's easy to see how parents' behavior has paved the way for demands like these to seem reasonable rather than invasive.

I am disturbed by how normal it has become to keep tabs on everyone's whereabouts, all the time. Parents track kids, kids track parents, spouses track each other; even close friends and adult siblings share locations.
The level of independence they have correlates to their trustworthiness; the more reliable they are, the more leeway they will get.
